description: We’re bhAvani, a multidisciplinary team interested in turning NASA’s open data and real-world space challenges into practical, creative solutions. Our strengths span software, AI/ML, cybersecurity, data analysis, web development and problem-solving. We’re looking for curious teammates who bring strengths in space science, Earth science, design, hardware, storytelling or data and who enjoy building, experimenting and learning together.
summary:
FLARE (Fire & Life-safety Analysis and Risk Explorer) is an interactive AI-assisted platform that transforms NASA’s microgravity combustion research into actionable fire-safety insights for future human space missions. The system brings together experimental combustion data, visualizations, and machine-learning-assisted analysis to help users explore how factors such as fuel, oxygen, pressure, temperature, and microgravity conditions influence flame behavior.

Instead of requiring researchers or mission planners to interpret large amounts of experimental information manually, FLARE organizes findings into an accessible interface where users can compare experiments, identify patterns, explore anomalous behavior, and understand potential fire-safety implications. The platform is designed as a decision-support and research tool for astronaut safety, helping bridge the gap between complex combustion research and practical mission planning.
details:
FLARE is an interactive research and decision-support platform designed to make microgravity combustion research easier to explore, compare, and interpret.

The project addresses the challenge by converting experimental combustion information into a structured interface where users can examine relationships between experimental conditions and observed flame behavior. Users can explore available experiments, compare relevant parameters, visualize results, and identify patterns that may contribute to fire risk during human spaceflight.

The core workflow consists of data collection and preprocessing, structured extraction of experimental parameters, exploratory data analysis, visualization, and AI/ML-assisted interpretation. Depending on the available NASA datasets, the system can analyze variables such as fuel type, oxygen concentration, pressure, temperature, gravity conditions, flame characteristics, and experimental outcomes. The platform is designed to surface relationships and anomalies while keeping the underlying experimental evidence visible to the user.

A key design principle is explainability. Rather than presenting an unexplained AI-generated risk score, FLARE connects observations to the underlying experimental conditions and provides context for why a particular pattern may matter for fire safety.

The intended users include researchers, students, mission planners, and engineers interested in combustion and human spaceflight safety. The long-term vision is to make experimental knowledge more accessible and support faster identification of potentially important fire-safety scenarios.

The project uses Python for data processing and analysis, with libraries such as Pandas, NumPy, Matplotlib/Plotly, and Scikit-learn where appropriate. A web-based interface can be implemented using a lightweight Python framework such as Streamlit or Flask, allowing the analysis to be explored interactively.

The creative aspect of FLARE lies in combining scientific data exploration with AI-assisted interpretation and safety-oriented decision support. Rather than building a generic visualization dashboard, the project focuses on translating complex microgravity combustion research into an understandable workflow: experiment → evidence → pattern → interpretation → safety insight.

The team also considered scientific traceability, uncertainty, usability, and avoiding overclaiming conclusions from limited experimental data. AI-generated interpretations are therefore presented as analytical assistance rather than replacements for scientific validation.
